..(Wednesday night through Monday)
Issued at 400 AM EDT TUE SEP 15 2026

The extended portion of the forecast remains on track with the
idea of a large 5h ridge weakening and drifting southwest a bit
through the rest of the week and into next weekend. This could 
perhaps include the eastern Gulf or coastal southeast region
becoming more active late in the period - not necessarily a 
recipe for helping to clear a 5h ridge to the north. The net 
result will continue to mean temperatures staying unseasonable 
warm and a limiting factor to the potential for widespread rain 
for much of the time. 

The previous long term discussion follows:

Ridging remains the dominant synoptic-scale weather feature across 
the Eastern Kentucky for the duration of the long term forecast 
period. When the period opens on Wednesday morning, a nearly 600 
decameter ridge will be centered over the Tennessee River Valley, or 
just to the south of the forecast area. The strength of this ridge 
is quite impressive. These modeled geopotential heights rank among 
the upper echelon of model climatology for this time of year. In 
fact, mean LREF heights of 600 dm sit at the 100th percentile of 
the dataset. This signal has been present in the data for multiple
runs in a row, which bolsters forecast confidence. The proximity 
of this anomalously strong mid/upper atmospheric ridging should 
accordingly yield mostly dry and unseasonably warm sensible 
weather conditions across Eastern Kentucky. On Wednesday, expect 
high temperatures in the lower 90s, mostly sunny skies, efficient 
diurnal mixing processes, and overnight ridge-valley temperature 
splits. Valley lows in the mid/upper 60s should be sufficient for 
patchy fog formation near sources of water, while ridgetops and 
the more exposed western locales could stay closer to the 70 
degree mark.

Confidence in these dry/hot conditions is highest on Wednesday, as 
the parent ridging will be closest to the JKL CWA in this time 
frame. Large-scale subsidence and antecedent dry air throughout the 
column will largely limit the potential for meaningful convection in 
the initial stages of the period. The dry air (and mixed afternoon 
dewpoints) should also prevent Eastern Kentucky from reaching heat 
advisory criteria. Apparent temperatures peak in the upper 90s, but 
remain largely below the triple digit mark. The heat continues into 
Thursday, with similar forecast highs in the lower 90s and heat 
indices in the upper 90s. While this may be enough to break the 
record high at the Jackson climate site, this is only because the 
previous record is a "weak" 90 degrees. The pattern actually looks 
to shift a little bit on Thursday, and that shift will eventually 
culminate in relief from the heat.   

As the ridge retrogrades west a little bit, return flow around its 
northern periphery will advect a plume of modified Gulf moisture 
towards the CWA on Thursday. The presence of this moisture will 
likely make it feel a couple of degrees warmer outside in the 
western third of the CWA. Those western counties will remain closer 
to the center of the ridge and thus under more of its influence. 
Locales situated in the Bluegrass and near Lake Cumberland could 
flirt with triple digit heat indices on Thursday, but this is 
unlikely in counties further to the east. Isolated to scattered 
general thunderstorm chances re-enter the forecast on Thursday 
afternoon for locations along and east of the Pottsville Escarpment. 
Similar, sub-50% PoPs remain in the grids through the weekend, 
largely modulated by the diurnal instability cycle. These could 
provide some localized pockets of relief from the heat before a more 
robust pattern shift emerges early next week. The forecast guidance 
suite continues to disagree on how exactly that pattern change 
unfolds, but there is a notable increase in the spread between the 
25th and 75th NBM temperature quartiles on Sunday and Monday. This 
affirms the notion that the increased rain chances correspond with 
increased forecast uncertainty surrounding the heat in the latter 
stages of the period. However, there is a better-defined downward 
trend in the temperatures early next week, with more compact model 
spread and median values back in the upper 70s/near 80 degrees.
